name: Survicate
tagline: Website, product, email, and mobile surveys with feedback analytics

pricing.basis: paid plan; billing basis requires review
pricing.native: Public paid plan exists; amount not safely recovered
pricing.notes: The official pricing URL is recorded, but a stable current amount was not safely recoverable in this pass. Do not publish a number until rechecked.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 25 responses/month; maximum 1,000 stored responses across active surveys; maximum 300 stored responses/survey; no data export.

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: 500 responses/month; 1,500 data points/month; 2 active surveys; 6-month retention; 5 seats; 1 team; 1 workspace; 1 folder; 3 AI chats; 25 integrations.
tiers.notes: Current official help documents this plan; it was not shown as a primary card on every pricing-page view.

tiers.name: Growth
tiers.limits: Starts at 250 responses/month; 1,000 data points/month; unlimited surveys; 10 seats; 2 teams; 1 dashboard.

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: Custom annual response/data allowance; custom seats; 10 dashboards.
tiers.notes: Starts at $349/month; monthly and annual contracts exist, but the exact annual-equivalent rate was not publicly exposed.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom response/data allowance, seats, dashboards, security and service levels.
tiers.notes: Starts at $569/month; monthly and annual contracts exist, but the exact annual-equivalent rate was not publicly exposed.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 25 responses/month; maximum 1,000 stored responses across active surveys; maximum 300 stored responses/survey; no data export.
pricing.billingTerms: Starter is monthly; Growth is publicly shown as annual; Pro and Enterprise can be monthly or annual, with exact annual discounts dependent on configuration.
pricing.hiddenCosts: Starter incurs response overages after 500 responses/month, but the rate is not publicly stated; higher-tier prices rise with response/data volume; the free plan stops collecting when its cap is reached.

verdictSummary: The visible customer feedback loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Survicate earns its keep through delivery, integrations, compliance, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a customer feedback tool with a schema-based form editor, public share link, validation, response table, CSV export, and webhook.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: SMTP or transactional email key in .env
whatYouLose: spam and abuse defense at scale
resilient polling of malformed and rate-limited feeds
whyPeopleStillPay: Survicate: Customers pay for dependable collection, spam control, notifications, integrations, and confidence that responses will not disappear.
ongoingBurden: Own storage, webhooks, email delivery, spam, file uploads, privacy requests, schema changes, and uptime.

priorArt.name: HeyForm
priorArt.desc: Open-source form builder and collection backend.

alternatives.name: Formbricks
alternatives.desc: Serious survey machinery without the enterprise invoice; self-hosting still means owning the machinery

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Survicate is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Survicate, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a customer feedback tool with a schema-based form editor, public share link, validation, response table, CSV export, and webhook.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: spam and abuse defense at scale; large integration and template catalog; compliance controls and guaranteed delivery.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
